Our national employment service has no local office at Seven Islands as yet. For several months consideration has been given to the opening of an office there. When our employment service operates at Seven Islands it will be its policy to provide equitable distribution of jobs as between workers from Quebec and workers from the Atlantic region.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement about the cost of living index as at April 2, 1951.
Ordinarily this announcement would be made through the newspapers by the dominion bureau of statistics. But in view of the fact that we have just concluded a debate on the cost of living and are still debating the budget resolutions, I thought it appropriate to make this month's announcement in the house.
I shall first read the announcement prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics, and then I shall make a few comments about the price of butter, which accounted for most of the change.
The following is the text of the dominion bureau of statistics official announcement:
The dominion bureau of statistics cost of living index advanced from 179-7 to 181-8 between March 1 and April 2. Nearly one-half of this increase of 1-2 per cent, or 2-1 points, was accounted for by butter which moved to high levels during the latter half of March and the early part of April, and then dropped sharply. The balance of the increase was largely due to other foods, clothing, home furnishings and miscellaneous items. The food index rose from 233-9 to 238-4. There were numerous but slight increases in foods other than butter, although decreases were registered for eggs, pork, and fresh vegetables. The clothing index moved from 196-3 to 198-8 following advances in men's wear and footwear. Increases throughout home furnishings were sufficient to raise the index of home furnishings and services from 188-6 to 190-7. The miscellaneous index advanced from 137-8 to 138-8 as a result of higher indexes for personal care, transportation and theatre admissions. Higher prices in some centres for coke and electricity raised the fuel and light

index from 146-5 to 146-7. Rents were not surveyed during April and the rent index remained unchanged at 137-6.
In the course of a speech in this house on April 9 during the debate on the cost of living, I said that "a preliminary survey of March prices indicates that the index will hold about even during March, or at the worst show an increase for that month of not more than one-half of one per cent". Actually the increase was, as I have already announced, a little more than one per cent.
The forecast of a smaller increase in the cost of living index between March 1 and April 2, anticipated a more rapid decrease in the price of butter than occurred. It was expected that butter prices would fall from the high point reached during the latter half of March to an April 2 price which would have been very close to the March 1 price. Actually, while the April 2 price was well below the March high, it was not until the second week of April that prices had1 again fallen to March 1 levels. If the mid-April price for butter -had been established by April 2, the cost of living index for that date would have shown an increase of less than one-half of one per cent.
Thus, this latest cost of living index increase was largely due to an increase in the price of a commodity which is now selling below the level of two months ago.

Resolved, that It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide:
1.	That the rate of the general sales tax be increased from eight to ten per cent and that the rate of sales tax on those articles at present subject to four per cent be increased to five per cent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just made a statement indicating that the cost of living index has gone up during the past month by 2Vio points. By way of explanation he says that it was because of the unusual advance in the price of butter in March. If I remember correctly, Mr. Chairman, the dominion bureau of statistics figures usually show butter and butter substitutes together. I wondered, although I did not take the trouble to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he made his statement, whether butter and other butter substitutes would not be considered as part of that whole effect which he says butter had on the cost of living. I do know that margarine made quite serious advances in price during that month, and kept quite even with butter in April.
There is one other comment that I should like to make with respect to the things I want to say about the budget resolution. It is this. When the full impact of the budget is made clear, let us say in a period of six weeks or two months, I am satisfied that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will have to show a much poorer picture than he was able to show today. From all that has been said here during the time that we have been discussing the budget and the budget resolutions, all that has been said by the minister and his

parliamentary assistant, it is clear, to me at any rate, that the government thinks it is essential to increase the sales tax by twenty-five per cent, and to levy a fifteen per cent excise tax on such things as stoves, washing machines, refrigerators and other household electric equipment, in order to get revenue for the defence effort.
These taxes are designed for one purpose only, namely, to get revenue, in spite of the fact that the immediate effect of their imposition is to add to the already serious inflation that devastates the people of Canada, and has been doing so for some time. I shall not waste the time of the committee by repeating the arguments that I and many others have already put forward, and put on the record, concerning the adverse effect of these taxes, especially on young people who are trying to get themselves established, and all those who have to exist on fixed incomes as well as those in the lower income brackets.
We have made known the reasons for our opposition to the sales and excise taxes, and it will not be necessary for me to repeat the arguments now. I do fear, however, that very soon the country will be faced with demands from all organized' groups for another round of wage increases. If further wage increases are granted, the cost of living will jump to new extremes. If, on the other hand, the increases are not granted, and especially if no effort is made to curb spiralling costs, along with the denial of further wage increases, the workers and producers of Canada can hardly be expected to feel like working harder and longer, as the minister warns they will have to do.
Let me say right here, Mr. Chairman, that I agree with the minister on that point. There is no way that I can see whereby production can be increased in this country except by all of us working harder and longer; and it is only through greatly increased production that the dangers of inflation can be averted at a time when we have to channel off, for defence purposes, large percentages of the things we do produce.
If Canadians will buckle down to it and will achieve in 1951 and 1952, let us say, as much as a six or eight per cent increase of physical volume of production-that is, of our gross production-it will be the greatest single factor, in my judgment, in bringing down prices and the cost of living. That is, of course, provided that we do not get foolish and allow the materials we do produce to filter away into other countries under foolish policies of one kind and another. But these taxes now, sales and excise, will not contribute in any way, in

my judgment, to an all-out production effort. My judgment is that it will result in discouraging production rather than encouraging it, and for that reason they are especially dangerous just now.
Whenever a government requires revenue, it is only good and common sense to go after that revenue where the money is. This government chooses to get the revenue solely by taxing for it. But the budget resolutions now before the committee propose to go after increased sales taxes and excise taxes in places where the money just cannot be obtained, without serious consequences to the people who are already overburdened with living costs, and who just cannot see how in the world they are going to keep their heads above water. The government has already admitted that single persons need not less than $1,000 and married persons not less than $2,000 to keep their heads above water. As a result the personal income tax exemptions are fixed at these levels.
Having admitted that, however, the minister turns around and seeks new revenue to the extent of $116 million from these people who are already overburdened. Then the minister proposes to tax away this year certain profits which corporations throughout the country have made. I have been making a special study of this whole corporation situation, and I should like to present that picture briefly today by way of showing to the minister that there is an alternative to which he can turn, and quite safely, to get his revenue. There is this alternative to which he can turn, if he actually requires it, although I believe the minister will agree-and whether he agrees or not, he knows I am correct-that when this fiscal year is ended he will have more than the necessary $116 million or $120 million by way of a surplus in revenue. I would bet my last shirt on that. He will have sufficient, and perhaps more than sufficient, to make up for what he proposes to get from these two taxes. I do not think there will be any doubt about that, particularly in the light of the fact that we are living in very buoyant times. Revenues are going to keep up.

These undistributed profits constitute a huge potential reservoir of funds for expansion purposes. Along with the minister, I think it is wise that undistributed profits such as I have mentioned should be there for expansion and resources development. Those things should be financed from this source as far as it will go. I agree with the minister when he says also that during the emergency years ahead he will have to put some sort of curb on reinvestment so as to help keep prices under control. If these $500 million of profits were left, even after a forty per cent surcharge, and were poured out into the field of reinvestment for development or expansion purposes, producing nothing while they are being spent for those purposes, the inflationary effect would be terrific. The minister is quite right when he says that he must impose some sort of curb.
I favour the profit motive to induce enterprise and productive effort. I have always said so. I believe that there has never yet been discovered a better motive for enterprise and productive effort than the profit motive. Out of those undistributed corporation profits most of the expansion of our production facilities which has taken place during the last four or five years was derived. The figures I have indicate that in 1949 the undistributed corporation profits were $601 million. I think it is fair to say that virtually all those profits have been reinvested in plant and equipment.
My own personal view is that it is not fair to say that corporation profits are unduly inflated in proportion to the increase in gross national production. To my mind the most important feature to be kept in view is the fact that the cost of living has been going up by leaps and bounds, while the pensions of old age pensioners, and payments made to others, seem to remain more or less stagnant. Therefore I am most anxious to see every possible dollar raised, whether it be by way of an excise tax or one on undistributed profits.
I am at a loss to understand why an hon. member from Alberta should be the one who would suggest that undistributed profits is a proper field for further taxation, when we realize that there is no province in Canada which requires more urgently moneys accruing from undivided profits for the development of its industries than does the province from which the hon. member for Peace River comes.
We need money for our poor people, too.

In the thirty years I have been here in this House of Commons I have never made a set speech. I rely on the hon. members who are listening to let me state some common sense once in a while. I sometimes wonder whether I am capable of expressing that. It reminds me of many long years ago when I was six years of age and I took the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington by one hand, and the hon. member for York East by the other, and we all toddled off to the little red school house. I was asked to get up to recite a piece after the teacher had drilled us in what we should say. I remember standing on the little platform while a little mouse crept out from a hole in the floor. I remember so well rising and saying:
I have a little friend who lives in my mouth,
He's as red as a rose and as warm as the south;
He has only one leg, but how quickly he goes;
My little friend tongue, as red as a rose.
I hope I did not have my little friend tongue in my cheek this afternoon when I registered my vote. I do not think I did
Excise Tax Act
because I am as satisfied as I stand here that I would sooner vote with the hon. member for a tax on undivided profits or corporation earnings or depreciation reserves than I would vote for an increase in the cost of living brought about by this 25 per cent increase in the sales tax. Someone in the chamber has said that this is a tax on the poor man. Mr. Minister of Finance, I am just as sure as I stand here that this is a tax on the poor man. Charge another dollar or two for each bottle of whisky we buy, whether we consume it ourselves or buy it for our friends, and put that into the treasury. Do that by all means.
The hon. member for Peace River was exploring around to find some way to offset the cost of living, and to make sure that pensions would keep some sort of pace with the cost of living. That is what I want to see happen. Not necessarily right up with it, but the compensation to pensioners should drag along with it. Let us have an objective in mind. If the cost of living goes up 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 80 per cent, why cannot this honourable government produce the mechanism and the mechanics within the confines of its organization to follow along?
If butter goes to 80 or 90 cents per pound, we have to buy it just the same. But pensions remain stagnant. To win an election you put out the baby bonus, and I suppose to win another election you can put out this new old age pensions scheme. I do not mind them playing with babies, as I love to play with them myself; but I object strenuously to any government or any individual playing with the finer sensibilities, as far as finance is concerned, of our older people. I think that is something-I am happy the Prime Minister is in his seat-that should receive prompt attention.	[DOT]
I plead with the right hon. Prime Minister to see that this Excise Tax Act which we are considering this afternoon produces immediately sufficient revenue so that the ideas that are in his heart and mind today with regard to looking after the old age pensioners will be accomplished long before he declares we are going to have another election in this country. It was rumoured that the baby bonuses were used to help win an election. God forbid that old age pensions should in any way whatsoever be used for a similar purpose. If they are, that action will react and boomerang against those who use it. I am hoping that that will not be resorted to.
Going back to excise taxes, I say to you, Mr. Minister of Finance-I am glad to see you smiling a little bit, as I like to see you in that mood-that your predecessor, the Hon. Charles Dunning, was not quite so happy

Excise Tax Act
when a proposition was made to him when he was sitting where you are now sitting with regard to how he, in common with the United States, could raise millions of dollars for revenue without hurting any particular industry but helping one industry that was native to this country. I refer to the Bailey amendment of 1936 passed in the United States which placed an excise tax of three cents per pound on every pound of vegetable oil imported into the country; as high as four and a half cents per pound and now one and a half cents per pound, with a quarter cent per pound duty. My reference to that indicates to my mind that the Minister of Finance missed an opportunity to raise anywhere from $2 million to $10 million by omitting to place an equivalent excise tax on the tremendous and ever-increasing imports of vegetable oil from Asiatic countries like Sumatra, Nigeria and Ceylon where the little pickaninny runs up a tree and shakes down a fruit which produces from 40 to 50 per cent of fats while the milkmaid in a dairy milks the dear old cow strenuously and gets only four to five per cent of the constituent butter fat, a part of margarine, if you want to call it margarine, which sells for 40 cents per pound, as my deskmate tells me.
What is it worth? Find out for yourself. When I was in Ceylon some time ago I saw what it is worth. I saw 15 pickaninnies, none over 12 years of age or weighing over 60 pounds, feeding into the trunk of a tree driqd out coconut which was producing 20 to 30 to 40 per cent of oil. The old mother sat on the veranda with a stick keeping them going and another boy kept the donkeys or burros moving. There were six of them, four being on the end of a pole going around and around . while the pickaninnies dropped in dried quarter sections of coconut and the oil was running out of the bottom of the stump into a four gallon discarded can which had originally belonged to the British navy or army or something.
I saw the father going down the road with a two-wheeled cart and a donkey in front dragging that black-as-muck coconut oil to the village. 1 saw them loading the oil on a ship to be shipped over here. I saw something else a few years ago which should make the members from Montreal stop and give some thought to the matter. I saw a tank steamer so heavily burdened with peanut oil from China at a cost of less than 3 cents per pound that she could not pull alongside the dock to unload. They had to lighter the ship in Montreal harbour. This was some years ago. The price is proportionate since but it is not 90 cent butter although it takes the place of it. They had to lighter the ship

in the harbour before they could pull it up to any dock in the city of Montreal to unload it. They unloaded it and the product was sold in Canada around 3 cents per pound. If my friend from Fraser Valley can unload creamery butter to compete with that he is good. It cannot be done.
I say to the Minister of Finance we missed a golden opportunity this year, when he needed excise taxes and money to pay all the current liquid indebtedness, in that we did not put ourselves at least on a parity with the United States and take a cent and a half a pound on every pound that came in. We would never have missed it. It would not have affected the price of butter. You would have had the money in the treasury, and I do not think very many people would have complained much about it. It is all on the record. I see that the well has gone dry. There is no water on my desk. We had better put a $2 tax on whisky and hope it will go dry too, and we will save the minister having to pass these rules.
Some ten or fifteen years ago we were exporting great quantities of bacon to the British market and the British people had control of the bacon situation. We in Canada were a bit worried that they might put some sort of tax on our bacon going into that country. We would have had three to four and a half cents a pound on vegetable oil coming into this country, and when you get above 200 or 300 million pounds a year of a cheap commodity of that kind made by cheap labour you cannot possibly compete against it. Let us be sensible about the matter. The product from which butter is made, milk, at the very maximum only produces 5 per cent butterfat. It is a pretty good cow that will give 5 per cent. I never saw one that would. It is more likely four and a half. When you try to compete against coconuts that produce 40 pounds of fat per hundred you just cannot compete.
The purification process used does not produce a loss of more than one or two per cent in the refining process. It is the simplest thing in the world to refine it. You can hydrogenate it to any consistency you wish from limpid water in the lower grades of the fatty acids up to a consistency as hard as oak by a simple chemical process which does not take anything away from the weight of the product. When you get it to the consistency where you want to use it as a substitute for lard, margarine or butter, then all you have to do is stop your hydrogenation process at that point. I do not like quoting figures, but I was told five minutes ago that margarine is selling at 47 cents a

pound. I should like to know whether there is 15 cents worth of vegetable oil in that 47 cents.
I should like to know what portion of the 47 cents is used for the high pressure advertising which comes over the radio and is to be found in every newspaper you pick up. As a chemist, which is my profession, I know that the product is inert and pure. I do not know anything about its vitamin content, but in these modem days vitamins can be added to the product, so they say. I take a vitamin pill once a day myself, although I do not know why. They say they can add vitamins to the product. I know that it is doing a job but I know that you do not grow coconut trees in Canada. I know that you do not have much success raising peanuts in Canada. I know that you do not have much success raising palm nuts or palm fruit in British Columbia. We are not in that particular temperate zone. Let us be sensible about it. Let us be at least half as sensible as our friends in the United States.
Even when we are hard up-and we are not as hard up now as we deserve to be- at least let us make sure that we keep pace with our commitments to deserving pensioners of all kinds. I make a special plea for old age pensioners because I am reaching that category myself. I am particularly anxious that we balance the budget. In considering the Excise Tax Act, I say to the Minister of Finance in as kindly a way as I possibly can that we are very happy that he has had surpluses, but anyone who has had the privilege of preparing a budget, no matter how small the business venture is, deserves to be criticized by his board of directors if he has a far greater surplus than he should have. I level that criticism at the Minister of Finance at this stage. I say to him in the same breath that with the cost of living so high, with the world picture so disturbed, with a background of three or four budgets as a result of which there were surpluses, this is not the time to budget for any very substantial surplus. If we had had deficits for the last four years I would not have made that remark, but I think, with the experience that the Minister of Finance has had, this is not the time to budget for a surplus.
This is a time when he should try to come out more even. This is a time when he should give some consideration to all the elements that go to make up our taxation system. This is a time when he should not disturb those who find themselves encumbered by paying that extraordinary 25 per cent increase in the sales tax. I think the second avenue I
Excise Tax Act
mentioned might have been explored, namely, vegetable oil. Perhaps I am guilty for not having brought it to the attention of the Minister of Finance in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Nevertheless we are on the record and two or three of the hon. members opposite me-I can see three of them in one glance-supported that issue right from the drop of the hat. We won our case before the tariff board and, as I said before, the only reason it was not imposed at that time was the fact that we did not want to disturb the British bacon market. I do not propose to move an amendment but at the same time I respectfully draw this matter to the attention of the minister and ask him to give some consideration to it. At the same time I again declare to you, sir, that I am opposed to this further increase in the sales tax for the reasons I have enumerated, and I hope that the minister will be able to see others.

Last Tuesday evening I
expressed opposition to this tax and suggested an alternative which I felt at that time was a reasonable one. I think the announcement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon that the cost of living index has now gone up to 181-8 makes it all the more important that we do not pass this amendment to the Excise Tax Act. If we do I think it is reasonable to suppose that in the next month the cost of living index will probably rise three or four points instead of two points as it did in the past month. It is pretty obvious from the debate that has gone on that members in all parts of the house do not like this tax, but some of them at least feel it is necessary because of the need for revenue. It is interesting to note that in introducing the tax-I am referring to paragraph 4, which imposes the duty on appliances-the minister said that tax was needed specifically for revenue. I quote from page 1812 of Hansard:
I regret that we can no longer afford to leave these entirely free of extra tax-
Later he went on to point out that this new tax would yield a revenue of $16 million. Like the leader of the opposition and others who have spoken, I feel that this tax might well be waived without giving us a deficit. I believe there is going to be a surplus sufficiently large that this tax may not be needed. But if we do accept the minister's statement that he must have this revenue I believe there is an alternative in the capital gains tax which would be less harsh on people in the lower income brackets.
I say at once that I do not like the thought of a capital gains tax in Canada. As the parliamentary assistant pointed out the other evening, there are numerous disadvantages

Excise Tax Act
in that it would be hard to administer, and it would probably discourage risk capital. But I suggest that even with those disadvantages it would be better lor the Canadian people as a whole to have a modest tax of that kind than the very harsh tax contained in paragraph 4 of this resolution. The other tax may be completely undesirable, but still it would be better than the one proposed. The parliamentary assistant suggested that the experience of the United States in connection with the capital gains tax had been very unfortunate. That may be quite true; yet it cannot be completely impracticable because there has been such a tax on their statute books since 1924. Some hon. members may wonder how the tax works there. As I understand, capital gains made by individuals or companies from the sale of any type of property other than normal stock in trade are subject to the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not like to interrupt my
hon. friend but if he will permit me I should like to raise a point of order. I really think a discussion of the capital gains tax would be very much more appropriate under the income tax resolution or bill. My hon. friend has put forward the view, as he is entitled to under this resolution, that we should have a capital gains tax instead of a commodity tax as is suggested here; but I suggest that a discussion of the merits of the capital gains tax or the economic impact of such a tax should be carried on under the other resolution. If we do not proceed in that way I really begin to despair of ever reaching any finality in the discussion of these resolutions.

I am inclined to largely
agree with what the minister has said. However, in a moment or two I am going to move an amendment which would substitute the capital gains tax for paragraph 4 of the resolution. Therefore I feel I have to give a little explanation of what I am trying to do.
I was saying that in the United States short-term gains, those made in six months or less, for income tax purposes are treated exactly as though they were additional income. Long-term gains are taxed at the rate of twenty-five per cent. I say at once I do not think that would be necessary at this time in Canada, but I do suggest that there is a place in our income tax structure for a modest capital gains tax. Therefore I move:
That clause 4 of the proposed resolution be deleted and that the following be substituted therefor:
"That it is expedient to introduce a measure to impose taxation on capital gains to the extent of $16 million so as to maintain the balance of ways and means."
[Mr. Thatcher. 1

I was just wondering if the
minister was going to reply to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition that he actually did not need this extra revenue. The leader of the opposition suggested that the minister was going to have a substantial surplus, and I am rather inclined to think he may be right, going by our experience during the last five years when we had very substantial surpluses that were not anticipated. I wonder, too, about the suggestion I made to the parliamentary assistant the other evening, as to whether any consideration was given to broadening the base for the application of the sales tax, rather than increasing it. It seems to me we have done some very good things in removing the tax. We have taken it off electricity, for instance, but on the other hand it seems to me that electricity used in business signs such as those advertising beer, for instance, might well be made subject to the sales tax. Then I think of building materials, from which the tax was removed. At the same time about half our building materials go into construction used for entertainment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Most of it is free of sales tax.

That is what I say. After all, a tremendous amount of building material goes into structures which definitely could not be classified as essential. So I was wondering if the minister had given consideration to broadening the base of this tax. As the Minister of National Revenue knows, he has a book about a foot thick listing all the things that are not subject to sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to answer my hon. friend's questions, because I have always conceived that the major function of this discussion in committee is to answer questions rather than to make speeches. As to his question whether consideration was given to broadening the base of the sales tax, I have taken the position that with the exception of cortisone and ACTH there would be no further extension of the exemptions. Now to answer the question as to whether I intended to reply to the point raised by the leader of the opposition, that I was raising more money

than I needed, I have attempted to reply to that matter on at least a dozen different occasions. 1 have stated my considered view that I am not trying to raise more than I need. I try as much as I can to avoid repetition. I am willing to sit here and listen to views reiterated time and again, but I really do not feel that I should detain the house by answering those points more than once.

I do not know whether or not I am in order, but I shall proceed until I am told I am out of order. Strangely enough, I am not going to talk about frigid-aires or anything like that. I am going to be very brief, but I should like to say a word or two about the dairy industry, in connection with the excise tax on imported vegetable oils. I would like to move an amendment, but in view of your ruling, Mr. Chairman, apparently I am not entitled to do so.
In my opinion the dairy industry is rapidly being put out of action in Canada. I am surprised that far more interested and more capable speakers than I, coming from Ontario and particularly from Quebec, have not emphasized that matter already. Apparently the government do not fully realize the seriousness of the position of dairymen in Canada. Apparently the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the bankers association do not appreciate that the dairy industry is rapidly being wiped out of existence. It may not sound very important to some people, but in the years to come I think they will find just how important our 550,000 dairymen are to this country. I know I am supposed to be a little hipped on margarine, but in what I have to say I am not going to discuss its merits or demerits except to the extent that it is affecting the dairy industry. Some years ago I endeavoured to the best of my ability to prevent either the sale or importation of margarine in Canada, because representing a constituency with a large dairy industry, and going on the advice of those who had made a study of that industry, I could see the effect it would have. For the life of me I cannot understand why the Department of Finance has not put a tax on imported oils. I well remember when the hon. member for Moose Jaw brought up the matter of restrictions that were put on the importation of small automobiles from England. That was soon brought into effect by the Department of Finance in order to protect the motor industry.
I was objecting to it.

I said the hon. member brought the matter up, as he would know if he would just listen carefully. For all I know, it was necessary that the action be taken that 80709-169*
Excise Tax Act
in fact was taken by the government in that connection. My point with regard to it is this. We act quickly when the matter concerns motor manufacturers; and we act quickly when it concerns textile manufacturers.
It was necessary.

I am not saying that it was not necessary. I am glad I am going to have some assistance from an hon. member from a mining district who is not as interested as are some other hon. members from Saskatchewan and Ontario in the manufacture of butter. I do not say it was not necessary to the employees or to protect the manufacturers. What I say is that the Department of Finance immediately grasped the subject and took action. The textile producers are well protected and well cared for. But apparently the dairy industry in Canada is to be thrown to the dogs. Is it not worth while protecting? It must not be forgotten, Mr. Speaker, that these vegetable oils, which are imported and used; in the manufacture of a substitute for butter in the form of margarine, can also be used to manufacture ice cream, milk for sale for human consumption over the counter, and other diairy products. The ruling of the privy council was adverse to the welfare of the dairymen of Canada. Apparently the long view has not been taken to protect this industry of over 500,000 actual dairy farmers and, I understand, many thousands of small creameries. But for the benefit of five or six manufacturers of margarine, this cheap oil is allowed to be brought in. For the benefit of one of the New Brunswick members, may I point out that I am not saying whether margarine is good or bad in this case. I am trying to speak purely for the benefit of the dairy farmers and creameries.
Nobody can tell me that we produce coconut oil in Canada. Last year we brought in roughly 10 million pounds of coconut oil- and I am speaking of pounds, now-produced by the class of labour described by the hon. member for Danforth. I wish the government would see fit to send me on one of these trips, so that I might view these things at first hand. I am still hopeful that I shall be sent as an envoy across to Hull or to some place at an equal distance, with all expenses paid.
I have here some figures with regard to the consumption of oils and fats in margarine, January-September, October-December, and total for 1950. These figures are in thousands of pounds, and all figures are on a refined oil basis. This is going to take a

Excise Tax Act
little bit of time; but in a limited way and, I will admit, with limited ability, I am trying to say something which I think is of great importance at this time if we are to admit openly, as apparently do those who prepared part of the budget, that we are willing to throw the dairy industry to the wolves in Canada. These figures are of vital importance. As to vegetable oils, from January to September, 1950-and these figures are in thousands of pounds-we put into margarine 5,621,000 pounds of coconut oil; in the fourth quarter, the figure was 2,236,000, making a total of 7,857,000 pounds of coconut oil that went into margarine in the year 1950.
Possibly some of the hon. members who do not believe in protecting the dairy industry know where they can produce that coconut oil in the Dominion of Canada; but I may say that I do not know. Certainly it cannot be produced in the Fraser valley. Then as to cottonseed oil-and I should like to know where that oil is produced in Canada-from January to September, 1950, 32,717,000 pounds were used in the manufacture of margarine, and in the fourth quarter, 9,389,000 pounds, making a total of 42,106,000 pounds.
I now come to soybean oil. A certain amount of soybean oil is produced in Canada. We had better look to the Minister of Finance ^because he has these experts who know all these things. They must know all these -.things or how could he not arrive at an excise tax on imported oils? He therefore would have right at his finger tips the figure as to how much soybean oil was produced in Canada. The total amount used in margarine last year, was 18,187,000 pounds; and the total amount of sunflower seed oil so used was 3,178,000 pounds and of other vegetable oils, 965,000 pounds.
As I see it, Mr. Chairman, the matter boils down to this question: Is the dairy industry to be maintained in Canada or is it not to be maintained? There is no other alternative. This has nothing whatever to do-and I again repeat it-with the merits or demerits of margarine. The question simply is whether it is worth while to maintain the dairy industry in Canada or whether it is worth while to build up a vast fortune for some six concerns, as the hon. member for Danforth says. He knows better than any other member of this committee the details of this business. Through experience, he knows the details; I do not. I doubt if any other member in this chamber knows the processing details in connection with that particular line of business. I do not know what the solution is, but
[Mr. CruickshankJ
I would certainly have an amendment, if it would be in order, to the effect that an excise tax be put on these oils.
Mr. Chairman, when it is said that this is a cheap substitute for natural butter, I would just ask you to bear in mind that when butter went up in price these oils imported in 1950, which went into the manufacture of margarine, went up; and up went your margarine three cents a pound. Just remember that, Mr. Chairman.
Ten cents.

Ten cents or whatever it was. I think every hon. member in the chamber will agree with me that it is obvious that this product, which was supposed to supplant butter with those who were unfortunately not able to pay the price that butter had reached, namely margarine, went up in price after that oil was imported; and as I pointed out, some ten million pounds of coconut oil alone from the cheap producing countries was used, with no excise tax whatsoever. It just does not make sense. Either the government, through the Minister of Finance, will have to admit that the dairy industry is to be thrown to the wolves or that it is not.
I am getting a little interruption here. Never since I have been here in the House of Commons have I been as serious about anything as I am with regard to this matter. I regret that I have not the ability to put before the committee what I should like to put before it. I hope that hon. members from Quebec and Ontario particularly will follow me and speak along these lines. I was sent back here to represent dairy farmers in the main. I myself own a dairy farm. I realize that my dairy farm and others in my riding are rapidly losing their value, as such, and1 will continue to do so if we are going to permit these oils to be imported as they have been. What would have happened if that experiment in west Africa, I think it was, had been successful with regard to peanut oil? Any hon. members who have read the history of that experiment know the quantity of peanut oil that could have been produced, and the cost at which it could have been produced, and the price at which it could have been sold. The hon. member for Danforth mentioned peanut oil. I have not here the figures as to the quantity that has been imported. Is that to be continued? If one of my colleagues were here he would say: I thought you were a free trader. I am still a

free trader, but we cannot have free trade just for one class of producer and not for others.
Speaking from memory, I believe we are permitted to bring in hay driers, litter carriers, and one or two other items, from the United States free of duty. In the current year that will not affect more than fifty farmers in my riding, but tens of thousands of farmers will be affected if vegetable oil is permitted to be brought in without a suitable tax being put on it. It is unfair competition. To carry it a little further- I do not like quoting figures, but incidentally these are authentic figures prepared in the bureau of statistics. Some of them were prepared through the courtesy of the dairy council of Canada. Incidentally, the dairy council of Canada represents all the dairymen of Canada, irrespective of where they come from. That council is guided by very responsible men, and they are particularly worried at this time, as they see the situation, as to whether the industry will be able to continue. Do not forget that the dairy industry does not include merely butter. It includes cheese, etc., and the necessary milk for human consumption on the fluid market.
For the year 1949-that is the latest year I have-the ratio of cows to population was as follows: Prince Edward Island, 2-1; Nova Scotia, 6-6; New Brunswick, 5-1; Quebec, 3-5; Ontario, 3-5; Manitoba, 3-2; Saskatchewan, 2-4; Alberta, 2-8; British Columbia, 11-9; average 3-7.
I cannot conceive why such a responsible organization as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which is familiar with all the bank reports published every month by the responsible heads of these banks, have not realized that it is not just a question now of talking about whether we like margarine or not. We are now talking about an industry that affects over 500,000 farm homes alone, as well as additional homes that are concerned in other ways with farm production. I am going to quote what the parliamentary assistant said, as reported at page 2595 of Hansard:
We must give some incentive to the people to put their money into venture capital, in our mines, in our forests, in aluminum plants and things like that.
Since these words were used by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance in this discussion I presume he was speaking for the Department of Finance. If that is true, it is not unreasonable for the dairy farmers to ask that they be given reasonable protection against the importation of oils which are produced in cheap labour countries
Excise Tax Act
on cheap land, with low taxes, and by people on a low standard of living. If the parliamentary assistant was expressing the policy of the Department of Finance in that connection, which he must have been-and I have no quarrel with his statement-surely it should carry forward and protect the dairy farmers of Canada. Always remember that of all the farmers in Canada the dairy farmer works the longest hours 365 days a year. He is-and I think even my wheatgrowing farmer friends will agree with me in this-the backbone of agriculture in the country. I am sorry that I cannot move an amendment. More than ever during my term in parliament I regret the fact that I have not the ability to put before the government and before parliament just how serious the matter is in my opinion. Either we maintain the dairy industry in Canada or we do not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When I get an invitation,
sir, from yourself, and from the Minister of Public Works, it is pretty hard to resist it.
The Minister of Finance suggested shortly after my colleague from Moose Jaw moved his amendment that your previous ruling, that on the amendment offered earlier today by the hon. member for Peace River, applied in this instance. As I recall, there were two aspects of the ruling you made an hour or so ago. In part that ruling dealt with the question as to whether or not an amendment in ways and means was in order if it proposed to substitute a tax in blanket form. The other aspect of your ruling had to do with the question as to whether or not a proposal for a tax that comes under income tax legislation was relevant when the matter of excise tax was before the committee.
I notice, sir, that you are nodding your head. I shall assume that I am correct that your ruling contained those two parts, and I shall now deal with them, in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance has suggested that the same ruling should apply to the present amendment.
With respect to the first part I think it is only fair that I be permitted to put on the record the fact that in recent times, to my knowledge, there have been four amendments of this type made in committee of ways and means. There may be others; but there are four, the records of which I have here.
On March 22, 1948, as recorded at page 2490 of Hansard, when the Excise Tax Act resolution was before us, I moved:
That clause 1 of the proposed resolution as amended and clauses 2, 3 and 4 be deleted therefrom, and that the following be substituted therefor:
"That it is expedient to introduce a measure to impose taxation upon excess profits to the extent necessary to maintain the balance of ways and means."
That amendment was allowed by the then deputy chairman, the present Senator Golding. Then, in 1949, as recorded at pages 1627 and 1628 of Hansard, an amendment was moved by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort, dealing with ice cream and similar commodities. That amendment was worded differently from the one in 1948. The 1949 amendment was ruled out of order by the deputy chairman, the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges. That ruling was the one that you, sir, as chairman of the present

committee, quoted an hour ago when you were dealing with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River.
The next amendment in the series is the one I moved only a few days ago, on April 26 of this year, as recorded at page 2415 of Hansard. My amendment on that occasion was:
That clause 1 of the proposed resolution be deleted and that the following be substituted therefor:
"That it is expedient to introduce a measure to impose an additional tax on spirituous liquors to the extent necessary to maintain the balance of ways and means."
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance took objection to that amendment on the ground that it should have given a specific amount. But you, sir, being in the chair on that occasion, although you did say you would like to have had time to think it over to a greater extent, nevertheless expressed the opinion that it was in order and you put the question.
Of the three amendments I have just quoted, two were allowed. Those two were in precisely the same language, using the expression, "to the extent necessary to maintain the balance of ways and means." One of those three, namely the middle one, which was ruled out of order, was worded in language different from that of the two allowed. I ask you to note that the one that was disallowed was worded differently from the other two.
The fourth of the amendments in these series is the one moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River. It was worded in the same way as the two that were allowed, namely the one I moved in 1948, which was allowed by Mr. Golding, and the one I moved last Thursday which was allowed by yourself.
You, sir, today chose to reverse your ruling of last week on the basis of the ruling of the deputy chairman on November 10, 1949. But in reversing your ruling you did say that what was wrong with it was that it did not set out a tax specific in amount.
I cannot quarrel with the ruling you made on the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River. I sought to do so, but I was stopped. My suggestion is, however, that the ruling you gave then laid down a point which has been met by my colleague from Moose Jaw. You said that what was wrong with the last amendment was that it did not set out a tax specific in amount. The hon. member for Moose Jaw has now presented an amendment which sets out the specific amount of $16 million, which is the amount which would be lost by dropping the tax on electric refrigerators, stoves and washing machines. Furthermore the amendment of the hon. member for
Excise Tax Act
Moose Jaw uses the key words which were held to be in order by Mr. Golding on March 22, 1948, and by yourself only last week, on April 26, 1951, namely the words, "to maintain the balance of ways and means."
I submit therefore that, with respect to the first aspect of the ruling you gave an hour ago, the point has been met and the amendment should be allowed. In this connection I think notice should be taken again of citation 500 in Beauchesne's third edition, which states:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
I think that at some point in our attempt to make an amendment based upon the right set out in that citation we should have the matter settled. If you have ruled that the kind of amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River today is out of order because it does not set out a specific amount, you should therefore rule the present amendment in order because it does what you ask, and does what citation 500 says is in order, namely it proposes to substitute another tax of an equivalent amount for that proposed by the government.
The government proposal is for a tax on electric refrigerators, stoves and washing machines which the Minister of Finance says will raise $16 million. The hon. member for Moose Jaw asks that that tax be dropped, and that there be a tax on capital gains to the extent of $16 million to maintain the balance of ways and means.
I leave that first aspect of your ruling of an hour ago-although by this time, it may be an hour and a quarter ago-and come to the second aspect of it, namely, as to whether it is good practice on a resolution dealing with the Excise Tax Act to move an amendment that seeks to alter both the Excise Tax Act and the Income Tax Act. I take it that any tax on capital gains would have to be imposed under the Income Tax Act.
In this connection I am going to rely on another authority, this time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has made statements on two occasions which I think are to the point at this time. Last evening when we were discussing procedure -we are spending a lot of time on that in this budget debate, and it could have been avoided so easily-I proposed that we deal with this present resolution in an orderly fashion and discuss it paragraph by paragraph even if we did not take a vote at the end of each paragraph. The Minister of Finance objected and said that the whole resolution was before us and as long as it was before us hon. members ought to be free to jump from a discussion of one tax to a discussion of another, or hon. members who were not here when one tax was up for discussion should be able when they came in to discuss a tax that had been discussed previously.
If the Minister of Finance takes that position I think he should be logical and the committee should be logical and realize that we have before us, not just the one resolution but the whole budget presented by the minister. When the minister finished his speech on the night of April 10 he did not present to the committee just one resolution, he presented several. He presented a resolution having to do with the Income Tax Act, one having to do with the Excise Tax Act-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
And one having to do with the Customs Tariff. That makes three, and1 three is several, so we are all agreed. There are three resolutions before this committee of ways and means. Furthermore, my same authority, the Minister of Finance, when speaking in the house on the budget on the night of April 10, as reported on page 1812 of Hansard, said:
If hon. members have succeeded in following my estimates of additional tax yields they will realize that my proposals so far leave me about $100 million short of my necessary objective of $400 million to balance this year's budget. My range of choice to secure this remaining $100 million is really limited to more than doubling the increase I have already proposed in the personal income tax, which could only be achieved by a sharp lowering of exemption levels, or an increase in the sales tax.
I do not agree with the Minister of Finance when he says that he is limited to two alternatives. However, I ask you to note that the Minister of Finance suggested that the point was reached where he had to decide between two forms of taxation to achieve a balance. Something was said the other night by Mr. Speaker about private members having the

same rights as ministers. We were discussing another point of order at that time. I submit that, if the Minister of Finance has the right to survey the whole field1 of taxation and decide whether he is to raise the money that he is short by taxation under the Excise Tax Act or by taxation under the Income Tax Act, the committee has that same right.
We now have before us three proposals, but we are dealing in particular with two resolutions, one with regard to the Income Tax Act and one with regard to the Excise Tax Act. We should have the right to register our decision. The minister has decided to raise what he is short by an increase in the sales tax and in other excise taxes. We suggest that some of the money that the minister proposes to raise under the Excise Tax Act should not be raised in that manner but should be raised by means of a capital gains tax, even though that comes under the other resolution. As a matter of fact, if the resolutions had been taken up in committee of ways and means in the order in which the minister put them on the order paper we would have dealt first with the Income Tax Act resolution. However, the minister proposed that we deal with this resolution first, which was his privilege.
My point is that the whole of the minister's budgetary proposals are before us. If there is any validity in citation 500 in Beauchesne's third edition-a similar citation will be found at page 431 of Bourinot-if there is any substance in the right of the committee of ways and means to propose an alternative so long as the balance of ways and means is maintained, the committee should be able to exercise that right in the form set out in the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.
To recapitulate, because the hon. member for Moose Jaw asks for a tax which is an alternative to the one proposed by the government, he is in order under citation 500. He meets the provisions of citation 500 and he meets the requirement you added this afternoon by naming the specific amount of $16 million. He meets the requirement that the balance of ways and means be maintained; he says so right in his amendment. As to relevancy, I suggest, as I have just been arguing, that we have all the minister's budgetary proposals before us and we should have the right to move a substitute tax as is contended by the authorities on procedure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I thank the hon. member for his able remarks. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw reads:

If the ruling were otherwise, the persons affected would not be aware of the rate of taxes to be applied to them. I think that my present ruling comes within the sense, if not the wording, of my earlier ruling. As a second ground, I rule that this amendment concerning a capital gains tax is not relevant to this Excise Tax Act resolution (see citation 344 of Beauchesne's third edition). AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. Nose worthy: Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as the Liberal majority in this chamber has decreed that we must take this omnibus excise tax resolution in toto rather than section by section, I And myself in the same position as other hon. members in the committee, namely, that I have no choice but to vote against the resolution in its entirety. I shall do that not because I am opposed to every section of the resolution but because I am so greatly opposed to certain sections, particularly paragraphs 1 and 4, that I cannot support the resolution. I was prepared to support a number of the amendments which you, Mr. Chairman, in your wisdom have decreed to be out of order; and I find that it would probably be difficult to move any amendment or to suggest any changes which will likely be acceptable.
I particularly want to deal with paragraph 1, that pertaining to the sales tax. I am opposed to the sales tax on fairly general principles; and I think those principles were stated very clearly by the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in a letter forwarded to the Prime Minister on January 17 of this year. It is not always that I find myself in agreement with the chamber of commerce-
They must be wrong.

-but in this particular I am. As to the sales tax, they say they are opposed to it on the ground that:
. . . indirect taxes are hidden taxes and as such are not conducive to public tax-consciousness and hence lead to indifference rather than careful scrutiny of government expenditures.
I think that is one fairly good ground on which to oppose the sales tax and, certainly, the increase in the sales tax which has been proposed in the budget.
I am opposed to the sales tax because I fail to see how that tax can have any other effect upon the cost of living than to increase it. I cannot see how that tax can be increased without, at the same time, adding further to the increased cost of living. Certainly with the cost of living rising, as indicated in the statement this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I suggest that we in

this parliament should be taking measures to halt or to reduce that cost rather than measures which, I think we must all admit, can do nothing more than raise that cost still higher.
To the extent that this increased sales tax raises the cost of living, it will give to workers across this country an added incentive to ask for increases in pay and we shall have that deadly spiral continuing. We shall be going on from one increase to another. To the extent that this tax raises the cost of living, it will also raise the cost of government. It will raise the cost price of those things that the government itself must purchase, and that increased cost will be felt in government at every level. It will be felt in increased cost of government at the federal, the provincial and the municipal level. Every municipal council across this country will find itself obliged to increase its mill rate because of this rising cost of living, to which the tax we have proposed in this present resolution will be a contributing factor.
I think economists are agreed that a hidden sales tax has the effect of retarding business. So far as it retards business, the government will lose in other forms of taxation possibly more than it will gain from an increase in the sales tax. I do not know just what consideration the minister has given to the extent to which an increased sales tax will retard business activity; but economists everywhere are agreed that that is the effect of a sales tax upon business. One hundred United States economists, in a signed statement to a former president of the United States, had this to say:
A sales tax reduces real wages, diminishes purchasing power, and puts a brake on industrial and business activity.
I submit that this is no time for us to consider the application of measures which will reduce real wages and diminish purchasing power of our people, and put a brake on industrial and business development. We have heard a great deal in this house, and particularly from members of the cabinet, concerning the need for increased production. We have heard a great deal to the effect that if we are to stabilize the rising cost of living, if we are to check it, we must do so by increased production. I submit that the increase in the sales tax will retard rather than increase production. It will have the effect of retarding production at a time when production is very essential.
A sales tax adversely affects the small businessman in contrast with larger business concerns. Here again we must agree that

larger concerns carrying a much greater variety of goods and at varying high and low prices are in a much better position to pass the tax on in the aggregate than is a small business. The tax favours big business, as do many other measures introduced by this government, and as do many other policies being followed by this government. I shall have more to say on that point later.
A sales tax again bears hardest on the poor, and those less able to bear that tax. Even with no sales tax on most of the essential foods, on certain building materials, and with other exemptions, the poor man who today has to clothe and house a family will find his tax bearing more heavily upon him than will the wealthy bachelor who has no one to clothe or to house but himself.
While certain essential articles are exempt from the sales tax, nevertheless many of the ingredients that are used in some of these finished products which are exempt are themselves taxed, and indirectly the sales tas has an effect upon the price of many of the articles that are supposed to be exempt from the tax.
Clothing, household furniture, children's clothes and shoes, are just about as essential in a country with our climate as is food. It is just as essential to keep a pair of shoes on a child's feet in this country as it is to keep a roof over that child's head. In taxing that clothing and many of the articles that are required in a home, the government is making it more difficult-more difficult than is necessary-for those who are attempting to keep homes together and to raise families in this country to do so.
Mr. John H. Gray, former president of the American Economic Association, has this to say regarding sales tax:
The sales tax is one more attempt to put the burden of taxes on the poor. It violates every canon of taxation accepted in the civilized world for 150 years.
It is a little surprising to find a Liberal government increasing the sales tax by 25 per cent. So far as I know the two other outstanding countries, except Canada, in the world today, that can boast of a 10 per cent sales tax are Russia and Spain. There is in both of these countries a 10 per cent sales tax. The Liberal government is certainly putting Canada in good company when it puts us in a class with either of those countries. As a matter of fact if the Liberals of this government-if there are any Liberals left in the government-were loyal or true to the professed principles of Liberalism they would have wiped out the sales tax altogether 80709-170i
Excise Tax Act
instead of seeking now to increase it. The one party that down through the years of Canadian history has most steadfastly opposed the imposition of sales tax has been the Liberal party. If you follow the history of the sales tax in other countries you will find that in every country and in every age it has been those governments that were farthest removed from the common people and who were most reactionary in their policies that have led the world in the imposition of the sales tax, led the way that this government is following at the present time.
Ways and means have been suggested to the minister from this side of the house whereby the sales tax, as referred to in clause 1, and the tax referred to in clause 4, could be avoided or alternative means of providing the necessary funds be found. The government has steadfastly refused to accept any of those suggestions. They will, in their steamroller style, force this Excise Tax Act through parliament. I do not doubt for a moment that, regardless of what the people of this country may think, those who sit on the Liberal benches will follow the direction of government ministers and vote to support this act.
If hon. members were duly concerned with the critical situation in which the country finds itself today, and gave recognition to the one control which parliament exercises over government, this government would not get a grant of even one dollar from parliament until some satisfactory steps were taken to curb the rising cost of living, instead of adopting measures that can only further increase that cost. If those sitting on the Liberal benches would consider, instead of government policy, the express wishes of the majority of the people in this country, they would line up with the opposition groups and refuse to grant one dollar to the government until steps are taken to check the rising cost of living.

small, and that they are left in a most unfavourable position so far as their stock of cigarette papers is concerned.

On May 10, 1909, as reported in the British Hansard starting at page 1463, Mr. Lloyd George introduced into the committee of ways and means a lengthy resolution having to do with various taxes on liquor at different stages. This resolution was quite complicated and it filled two full pages of the British Hansard.
After he had moved the resolution in committee the chairman apparently put it to the committee in its entirety and Mr. Austen Chamberlain objected. Mr. Austen Chamberlain suggested that it was a most complicated resolution containing table A, table B, table C, and then a breakdown of table C into two sections which were headed by Roman numerals, which in turn were broken down into sections headed by Arabic numerals and so on down the line. Mr. Austen Chamberlain took the view-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

One of your colleagues has a mortgage on commas. As I say, Mr. Austen Chamberlain took the view that as it was so complicated it should be discussed seriatim. Mr. Lloyd George then said:
May I submit to you, sir, that this resolution is purely a formal stage, with the view to authorizing me to introduce the finance bill, and that therefore I submit that it is proper that the whole of the licences should be included in one resolution, seeing that it is a formal stage to enable me to introduce the bill for licences in general.
Whereupon the chairman, Mr. Emmott, ruled on the point that had been raised by

the member for East Worcestershire, Mr. Austen Chamberlain. The chairman said:
It is quite true, as the right hon. member for East Worcestershire has said, that the time which I have occupied in reading this resolution has been quite an unusual draft on the time of the committee, but with regard to the question put to me as to the form of this resolution, my reply is that the resolution is such that I must take it as it is. I cannot say how far there is a precedent for a resolution of this length, but having regard to the fact that it deals entirely with licences for excise-able liquors, I cannot undertake to alter it.
Mr. Austen Chamberlain had some more to say despite the ruling of the chairman that he had no alternative but to accept it. A little later, however, Sir F. Banbury intervened and said:
I wish to raise a point of an important character. Would it be in order to move that the resolution be divided into two?

If you turn back to the first line of the resolution you will find that it referred to taxes or licences for the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquor, but by deleting the two words "and sale" all of the taxes in that resolution that referred to the sale of liquor would be removed, and the only taxes left were the taxes relating to the manufacture of liquor. The chairman accepted the motion as in order. It was debated at length and eventually was voted on at pages 1474 and 1475. The amendment was defeated, but my point is that the situation is on all fours with what we have here in the house now. I have not the citation under my hand, but I am quite sure there is a citation in Beauchesne, third edition, stating that by unanimous consent the committee may set aside the rule. First of all, I want to sympathize with His Honour the Speaker. I notice that he has quite a hoarse voice from disposing of the appeals that have been made against the rulings of the chairman. I feel satisfied that a number of the appeals that have been made would not be made if hon. members had a chance to express their opinion, or had the minister not brought in the iniquitous taxes contained in the resolution.
We have heard many times that Canada is supposed to be a Christian country. I am wondering whether Satan is not in control of the Minister of Finance, his advisers in particular, and those who are supporting him even in the votes here tonight and this afternoon. In this country we have many young men and young women who are working hard and honestly, trying to pay their way, pay their debts, and provide a decent standard of living for themselves and their families. We are told that the taxes are being levied at the present time for the purpose of guarding ourselves against the effects of communism. I am wondering whether the taxes that are to be levied, if the resolutions that are before us are passed, will not help to build up the communist organization in Canada. I have thought about that time after time during the past few days; in fact during the past week, I have thought about rising in my place several times and expressing this opinion. But we do not find any relief from the taxes. We are not even given a chance to vote on individual taxes as they are proposed by the Minister of Finance. I am not satisfied;

people throughout the country are not satisfied. And while we are in grave danger, tonight's issue of the Journal gives this warning:

One hundred per cent.

If you like, 100 per cent. Since it has been shown that there are other sources from which the minister could get revenue if he needs revenue to balance his ways and means, and since we have pointed out that the minister may not need any more revenue than he would get if he did not put on these two extra taxes, in the light of these facts we felt that it was our responsibility to the people of Canada to fight them just as long as it was possible so to do. We are not through yet by any means. We may have to yield on the resolution but there is a bill coming up. I am just serving notice now, and repeating what I said some days ago, that if this opposition which represents more than half the people of Canada will band together and fight for the principle we have been fighting for during the last seven days we can bring this government to the point where they will have to yield. That is all there is to it.
I for one am prepared to stay here until Christmas if that is necessary, to fight this battle for the people of this country. I am only saying that that is the reason we have put up this battle. We put it up because we were convinced in our hearts that these impositions should not be made at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

That is the job of the opposition parties. I do not think the people of the country are under any illusion that the opposition are not opposed to the government's financial proposals. What the opposition would do if they had the responsibility of putting forward the proposals is a different matter and one into which I do not propose to go. I am quite satisfied to have had this discussion and I do not criticize any hon. member for the time he has taken in presenting his point of view.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just a few words. First, I want to point out that if a vote is taken on this resolution It should be noted that it involves tax increases to the

extent of $194 million. It involves also certain tax decreases, but they amount to only $14 million. Since we are denied the right of voting on the sections individually and are faced with the necessity of voting on the resolution as a whole we have to look at it in its entirety. We see it as a resolution that grants relief of only $14 million by way of decreases but imposes $194 million by way of increased taxation. Since we have to take the resolution as a whole, good and bad together, and since there is so little good in it and so much bad, we are opposed to it.
In connection with the way in which the Minister of Finance proposes to raise his additional revenue, may I point out one significant feature. According to the table which he placed on Hansard at page 1814 we are given the amount in dollars which *the different increases in taxation will produce.
