speechtext:
For the full year the increase in the sales tax would be $125 million rather than $105 million; in the income tax, $158 million rather than $85 million; in the other excise taxes, $110 million rather than $89 million. It is true that taking these figures the percentages I want to give would be altered. I shall be perfectly fair and say that they would be different, but I have not
Excise Tax Act
the time to work out the percentages now that I am on my feet. But I want to give the percentages that apply in this year because after all that is what counts. Before we get to another fiscal year no doubt there will be other changes in the minister's fiscal policy. What we want to deal with now is the tax that applies to the fiscal year 1951-52, and these changes are indicated in the table that I have referred to on page 1814.
Taking the actual number of dollars which the minister proposes to get over and above the number of dollars he would have got if he had not made these increases, the results are that from personal income tax the increase would be 10-8 per cent; from sales tax, 21-2 per cent; and from the other excise taxes an increase of 37-3 per cent. If we were to take these two categories of excise taxes and put them together, namely, the general sales tax and the other excise items such as taxes on refrigerators, stoves, washing machines and so on, the over-all average of the excise taxes has increased the revenue to be taken from the Canadian people by 26-4 per cent. I ask that the committee set these two main figures alongside each other. The increased revenue to be taken by the treasury from the Canadian people on the basis of income tax, the tax that is nearer to being fair, the tax that is based on ability to pay, is only 10-8 per cent. The increase to be taken by taxes on commodities, the kind of taxation which is not based on ability to pay, is in the over-all picture an increase of 26-4 per cent.
It is my contention that even before these changes were made there was too large a proportion of government revenue taken in commodity taxes as opposed to the proportion taken by the fairer method, namely, the income tax. By the changes being made in this resolution along with the other one, that already unfair proportion is being made just that much worse. For this reason, as well as for the reason I gave earlier when I pointed out that the net effect of this resolution is $180 million increased taxation on commodities, we in this group are opposed to this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

Mr. Chairman, before we
vote, I wonder if members of the house yet realize what these imposts mean. There are tens of thousands of people throughout Canada who today are at their absolute wits' end to know how to live. Let it not be forgotten that the bailiff is on the job. He is

Excise Tax Act
going around from house to house, from street to street and threatening people with ejection from their homes. He is threatening to seize their furniture and sell it. Taxes in the communities are being increased, many of them will be increased still further by reason of these imposts, and the bailiff is around threatening their homes with seizure if they are unable to pay their taxes.
What is actually happening is that the Minister of Finance is thrusting his mischievous hands in the pockets of the people and taking out from them the very money which people have to have in order to be able to live. This is more serious than words can make it appear. The minister just smiles about it. I would think there is cause for tears. I know in the town in my constituency where I live there are a good many people who have already shed tears by reason of these imposts. If they were absolutely necessary it would be a different thing but they are not necessary, not by any manner of means. If we are managing our country on a financial system that makes measures like these necessary then the sooner we change that financial system the better.
Change the government.

Surely everyone can see
that something has gone radically wrong when a country as wealthy as Canada in every respect, with the type of people Canadians are, has to have imposts of this kind thrust upon the people even before we are at war. That is what we are faced with. I said a few minutes ago that this kind of measure is not necessary. I have already made two speeches on debt-free money during the last few days. A great many people have disregarded the speeches but let me tell them they disregarded those speeches at their peril.
Hear, hear.

I am not threatening anybody but if you once get the people in this country to the point where they begin to believe that it is absolutely impossible to elect a government that will rule them decently, then you can imagine what they will do.
A Social Credit government.

Of course. There is no
question about that. Social Credit will solve the problem. We have a lot of people who know as much about Social Credit as they do about what is on the other side of Mars. Yet they are laughing like silly fools, cackling like jackdaws. We have got to the point now where something must be done other than

the imposition of taxation measures like these. There are any number of people who will cackle away about the proposals of Social Credit but they have no arguments to offer against them. They do not dare to try to answer the arguments of Social Credit. The Minister of Finance does not dare to try to answer them. He does not dare to because he knows he cannot refute the arguments of Social Credit.
We are faced now with a situation where we must have money; we will all grant that. But to take money away from people by such a nefarious tax as the sales tax is a scandal to this nation. Let me just show the minister the absurdities that are involved. He has implied, and the bank managers all over the country, bless their dear hearts, have been trying to convey, that you have got to tax more in order to curb inflation. The minister has tried to get us to believe this taxation is an anti-inflationary measure, that one of the reasons for this tax is to oppose inflation. Why oppose inflation? Because he presumes that we have a shortage of goods in Canada, and the dear member for Greenwood supported him. "We have got too many dollars chasing too few goods" they say. He maintains or tries to pretend or establish the idea that we have a shortage of goods and too many dollars chasing the goods. He says that therefore we have got to take the dollars out of circulation so that the prices of goods will come down.
Let me just show you the kind of situation the minister is in, and let him figure his way out of it. At page 1762 of Hansard of April 9 the Minister of Trade and Commerce had certain things to say, and I ask all these people who know so much to listen to what is said here.
Oh, we hear you.
Go ahead.
Carry on.
The important thing is to use your heads for thinking instead of rattling something.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. May I ask the hon. member to address himself to the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, did you ask me to address you? I shall be happy to do so. I love talking to you, Mr. Chairman. Listen to these words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said:
I am sure that we can get along quite comfortably as consumers and still engage in a substantial defence effort. A few things may in the course of time become unavailable or relatively scarce, but standards of living will remain high. Unless all-out war comes. Canadians can continue to live well.

How many tens of thousands of people will these taxes make unable to live well?
Hear, hear.

There are tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, who are not now living well, and I defy the Minister of Finance to say they are. I defy any member on the government side to say they are. Hundreds of thousands of them are not living well now.
Where?

In Toronto, Montreal,
Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, Halifax, Vancouver, Victoria. Name all the cities in the country and you will find them by the thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Oh, oh.

The well-fed Minister of
National Revenue has quite a lot to say on these matters. It would not take me very long to guide him through Ottawa and show him thousands of people who are suffering right here in the city of Ottawa within a mile or so of this house. They are suffering, and this proposes to make them suffer more, though the Minister of Trade and Commerce has solemnly declared in this house that people in Canada do not need to suffer. How does the Minister of Finance figure his way out of this? That is what we want to know. He cannot do it. Is he prepared to contradict what the Minister of Trade and Commerce says regarding the supply position in Canada? If he is not, if he has to concede that his colleague knows what he is talking about, then the Minister of Finance cannot possibly justify the imposition of such taxation in order to decrease the cost of living.
Very well; one of the main reasons he advances or tries to suggest for imposing these taxes is completely swept away. Surely everyone can see that. His next argument is that we have to raise the money. Well, I am going to state once more, even at the expense of having a good number of shallow people laugh about it, that today this government can create the money the minister proposes to raise, every single dollar of it, with the power of the government conferred upon it by the Canadian constitution, and put that money into circulation without causing the slightest ripple in the price structure. Why do I say that? Because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out very clearly that we have enough goods so the people can live well; and certainly putting $400 million or $500 million more into circulation among the poor is not going to make them live any more than just fairly well. Those are the fundamental facts which confront us as Canadians.
Excise Tax Act
Now let me raise another point. This budget is laying down a principle; it is pointing the way. It is saying to Canadians that the bigger war effort they want the more of this kind of abomination they will have to take. Never mind if as a result you cannot buy your fuel. Never mind if as a result you cannot pay your rent. Never mind if as a result you cannot wear shoes. You have to pay these taxes and you are going to like it, because you elected a fine Liberal government which is going to see that you do. They have not sense enough to see any other way of doing it, so the people will have to go ahead and like it. That is what it means. The minister has laid this down very definitely. This is going to be a pay-as-you-go war. This means that no matter how much we can produce, no matter how great our resources may be, we cannot expand the war effort of Canada any further than we can get money by stealing it out of the pockets of the people and putting them in misery and poverty. In other words the principle which underlies this budget limits the extent of Canada's participation in defence. Let us see if anyone can answer that.
Some will say that when the war gets a little worse we will begin to borrow. When the war gets a little worse and we have to use more of our goods for the support of our forces abroad it will be harder than ever to continue a pay-as-you-go policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon. gentleman not to go so far afield from the subject under discussion.
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman; but as I see it the whole thing is centred right around this set of pernicious taxes.
Whether we are to tax or not; that is the question.

And whether we are going to be able to fight a war with our full force, whether we are going to be able to use all our manpower and material resources to fight a war, or whether we are going to be hamstrung and trammelled by finance. It is a certainty that if we get any more taxes like these the people of this country are not going to become prosperous as the war advances, and are not going to become any more able to pay taxes. This is more than serious. We are not faced with the kind of proposition we were faced with at the beginning of world war II or world war I. We are faced with a struggle for our very existence, against the greatest power we ever went up against. For us to sit here calmly and talk about this thing in this way is absolutely preposterous.

Excise Tax Act	*
Hon. members opposite are feeling quite unhappy because the opposition has put up a puny little struggle. What if they had been up against the kind of opposition William Lyon Mackenzie King put up against R. B. Bennett during the five years that man struggled against a depression which William Lyon Mackenzie King had helped to bring on? If this government had to carry on against an opposition such as William Lyon Mackenzie King and his party put up against the Conservative government in those five depression years they would know what opposition was. Beside that opposition the puny little efforts we have put forth during the last seven days would amount to small change. I happen to know. I do not know how many members now in the house were in parliament at that time; probably there are a few. I was told by one who was here that hardly a day went by when four or five or six Liberals would not ask questions of the government without ever giving notice; and that is just an example. That is the kind of opposition they had, just dirty, sordid opposition; just meanness. It is too bad to say that about men who have passed on, but that is what occurred. Yet the moment a little bit of effective opposition is put up against the Liberals today they begin to whine like babies; they call order, and all the rest of it.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I have said all I want to say on that subject. Now here is the reason we have so sternly opposed this measure. I am only sorry we are not better organized. I am not naming any particular group; I think on the spur of the moment we have organized a pretty good struggle, but if the whole body of the opposition including our Conservative friends had co-operated in this thing we probably could have got something for the Canadian people. But we are going to have to let this thing go

through because we are not organized to keep on talking. But when we let it go through-

I certainly desire to cooperate with you, Mr. Chairman, but after having been here for seven days and listened to the kind of thing we have had to listen to, and having had to look at the sad countenances of the government, reflecting their feeling of injured dignity, I am inclined to speak just a little bit freely. But I shall defer any such talk as that until a later time. May I commend you, Mr. Chairman, for the way in which you are handling matters.
I will just say this in closing what I have undertaken to say. Here is a set of measures which are pernicious through and through. There is not a commendable feature in any one of these sales taxes; neither is there one in the excise tax. If the desire is to limit the consumption of refrigerators and electrical appliances, rationing can easily be applied. If the desire is to eliminate consumption of any other kind in Canada, rationing can be applied. But there is no need for it at the present time. Rationing can be applied in two ways, either as the article is

being offered for sale over the retail counter or as the supply of raw material is being permitted to come to the factory. It is the simplest thing in the world to limit these things and save the use of necessary war materials. No reason at all under the sun can be given for these taxes. As I said, they are pernicious through and through; they are inflationary; and as a means of getting revenue, they are utterly unnecessary. I am opposed to them with all the energy that I have. Since we are probably not strong enough to go any further, I shall have to cease until I get another chance to talk.

No, Mr. Chairman.

Maybe so; but it will be a short one, anyway. I have been ready to vote on this resolution more than once, Mr. Chairman. Even yet we have had no evidence, or even no statement offered to us by the Minister of Finance, as to the absolute need for this tax. When we pointed out to the minister the years in which his excess collections of revenue have been not tens of millions or scores of millions but hundreds of millions of dollars, his answer, as I recall it, was that while it was true he had overestimated, nevertheless he had not overestimated much more than had the authorities in Britain, or in Ontario, or where you please. To me that is just the old argument of the pot and the kettle. So far as I can recall, the minister has never yet said a single word to deny the argument which has repeatedly been made here, namely, that if the gross national product is what he himself has estimated it to be, in all probability we shall have a surplus which will be more than enough to take the place of this reduction which we have asked.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We shall now consider the customs tariff resolution. Shall the resolution carry?

I wish to ask one or two general questions with regard to the tariff. When the minister spoke in his budget speech he referred to the meetings which had been taking place at Torquay and to the fact that no announcement regarding them could be made until, I think, May 9. The question that I want to ask the minister is this. Will he enlighten us as to the division of what I will call the tariff problem and tariff negotiations. We have had negotiations going on for months at Torquay, following previous negotiations at Annecy two years ago, I think it was, and negotiations at Geneva four years ago. I should like the minister to tell us something of the scope of those negotiations, explaining the relationship which they bear to the operations meanwhile of our own tariff board. I should also like to ask whether some of the proposals which are in the schedule to the resolution are the result merely of negotiations which have taken place with individuals. In other words, my question is really threefold. What is the scope of the negotiations going on at Torquay? I raise this question particularly by reason of whatever tariff changes there are affecting us and the United States. In the second place, what is the relationship of what is going on there to the operations of

Customs Tariff
our own tariff board? I am not quite sure whether it has been in abeyance or what it has been doing. Third, are any of the proposals in the schedule the result neither of what has been going on at Torquay nor of the proceedings before our own tariff board, but merely the decisions of our own department in negotiation with individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To answer the last question first, Mr. Chairman, none of the customs tariff proposals which are before the committee have any relation to the discussions at Torquay. The tariff changes which are made here are of some significance but they are not of wide application. I do not know that I can add much in general terms to what I said in the course of my budget speech. There are a number of items which come within the classification of farm implements, to which free entry is given under the proposed customs tariff resolution. There are new tariff schedules with respect to the plastic items which implement a report of the tariff board which I tabled at the conclusion of my budget speech. As to the discussions at Torquay, as my hon. friend has indicated, a concurrent statement will be issued on May 9, by the various countries interested. As to those negotiations, I can add nothing to the general statement that I made in my budget speech, but a full statement will be issued on the ninth. There will, I expect, be a statement in the house and a rather more complete press release issued at the same time.
As to the functioning of the tariff board, that board has been extremely active. It has been hearing a great many appeals. There have been a great many references. In the absence of the chairman of the board, Mr. Hector McKinnon, at Torquay, the deputy chairman, Mr. Leduc, and the other member of the board, Mr. Buchanan, have been sitting as a board. I do not think I can add anything more than I have said in the general statement on the tarifE proposals.

I have one
supplementary question. There are certain tariff concessions to the United States. I am not questioning these now. They seem to me, as far as my knowledge goes, to be reasonable, but it raises this question in my mind. Did we get any quid pro quo for them? It raises also this question. In our negotiations at Torquay are we, or are we not, in a better position when everybody is seated around a table to get a quid pro quo? A third addition to the question is this: What is the division which results in the fact, as I understand it. that these changes that you have now made are made without quid pro quo? The minister will inform us on that. If without quid pro

quo then my question is, are we in a better position to get a quid pro quo at Torquay and further, if that is so, why are these particular matters not the subject of negotiation at Torquay?

Just one
further question. I mean, they might not have very much weight and yet it is hard to-

speechtext: At the time we prepared these tariff proposals we knew what we were going to get at Torquay, and we knew what we were going to have to give. I have one example on the
point which the hon. member for Greenwood

has raised. I think sprinkler irrigation systems come under item 409f. We have had some young men establish a plant in Vancouver to manufacture sprinkler irrigation systems. They are just getting nicely into the business and are able to meet the demand when suddenly these sprinkler irrigation systems are deprived of protection. They lose any protection they have, and yet there is no removal of the United States duties; with the result that that firm probably will be put out of business. They cannot get into the United States market because of the high United States tariff, and yet Canada takes her duty off and allows the United States firms to wipe out that business.
I do suggest to the minister that that particular item might have been held until some reciprocal arrangement was made with the United States. There is no reason why we should allow their sprinkler systems in free when they will not allow ours to go into their country. For all the difference it would have made to the users of these systems, I do suggest that a mistake has been made on this particular item. The removal of the duty should be delayed until an attempt at least is made to have the United States take off their duty. Surely to goodness the Canadians should be on the same basis as the people of the United States. Why should we be unable to sell our goods to them? The handicaps are big enough even if the duty is the same on the goods going each way. There I think is a case where there should have been negotiations and an attempt made to get the United States duty taken off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am familiar with the situation to which my hon. friend refers. I was aware of it before we arrived at the decision to include the items in question. The United States negotiators were not interested in a tariff concession here, and the decision to remove the tariff on these items was made in line with the basic policy decision taken in 1944 that agricultural implements and articles used in agriculture would be free of duty. My hon. friend will recall that Mr. Ilsley announced that policy. Since that time, it has been: urged upon us that various specialty items, such as sprinkler systems, are used, and extensively used, in agriculture-and these irrigation systems come within that category.
I know the firm in British Columbia which has just started. I am sorry that the removal of the tariff should come just at the time when it is getting going, but as the committee knows, I am not one of those who believe in the infant industry theory; and I do not want industries created behind a tariff wall which may create problems in the future.
Customs Tariff
Careful consideration was given to this particular item, and a decision was taken that it should be included in the agricultural group to which I referred.
What is almost sure to happen is that once the United States firms get this Canadian firm out of business they will be in a position to charge whatever they like to the Canadian farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we will recognize that it is unlikely that there will be widespread manufacture of this type of equipment in Canada. There never was, up to a year or so ago. Unfortunately, the United States tariff is, on the average, very much higher than ours. That is one of the great disabilities under which we labour here. We have a relatively low tariff; they have a high tariff; and that is why we have been so anxious in these succeeding discussions at Geneva, Annecy and Torquay to whittle away at the United States tariff; but nevertheless, whatever their tariff may be, in this country we have adopted the policy that so far as agricultural equipment and implements are concerned, they come in free.

I think one reason the policy has been adopted is that leading Canadian farm implement manufacturers are able to stand on their own feet and ship throughout the world. But, as the minister said, this is a special type of product, and it is not in that category at all.
We are going to have a big aluminum development in central British Columbia within the next two or three years. I believe these sprinkler systems are made of aluminum, and there will be need for a market for that product. I hope the minister will give some further thought to this item because it is unfair that the Canadian producer should be placed in the position where the Americans can come in and wipe him out, but he cannot get into the American market at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am looking at this particular situation again in connection with another matter, to see whether on parts, and so on, any assistance can be given to that industry.

The Americans subsidize the export of apples to Canada and other countries to the extent of $1.25 a box. That artificial competition quite recently caused the British Columbia fruit growers to sell about 100,000 boxes to Ontario and Quebec cu, auoui a aoiiar a oox, wmca is- very little more than the cost of packing and of the boxes. Does he consider that a subsidy that creates artificial competition with Canadian fruit is in keeping with the spirit of the Geneva agreement?

Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not aware that such a subsidy existed. However, the hon. member knows more about that business than I do. As he is no doubt aware, the tariff on Canadian apples going into the United States is very much lower than the tariff on American apples entering Canada. That is one of the relatively lew cases where the American tariff is lower than our own. However, I have to look at the type of export subsidy to which he refers in order to see how it is affected by the Geneva agreement.
Will the minister check that matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question regarding item 409f. While it deals with a wide range of agricultural machinery, I am interested particularly in grain or hay driers. A year ago some farmers in my constituency imported grain and hay driers. When they consulted the department they were told that because the equipment was for agricultural purposes it would be admitted free. Once it was landed in London, however, the duty was charged, and they had to pay it.
I came to Ottawa to protest, and the duty was paid under protest. I see by this item that this equipment is now admitted free. Is there any chance that these people will receive a refund in respect of those articles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not. I gave pretty careful consideration to the driers to which the hon. member has referred. After discussing the matter with my tariff advisers I came to the conclusion that this equipment was pretty much outside the ordinary range of agricultural equipment or implements, and took us into a completely new field. I will add that it was something I felt that in another year I might consider further. But I had to get a great deal more information as to what similar items might be affected before I would be prepared to remove the tariff. Therefore I think I could say clearly that this year I would not be prepared to make a recommendation to eliminate the tariff on those articles.
I note that under item 409f they are now free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not quite sure as to the exact part to which the hon. member is reierring.
I am referring to tariff item 409f.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am fold that this covers driers except what are described as big bins.
The fans and motors are included?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I might point out that in Iceland there are more hay driers used than in all Canada. With their wet weather they have become almost a necessity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will look at it another year, but that has been why we have decided against it.

I should like to support what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to apples. This was a case where British Columbia had virtually to dump apples in Ontario at a loss, and this I believe was the result of subsidized American exports.
Then I should like to refer briefly to the question of vegetable oils entering this country. This afternoon during the discussion of another resolution the minister said that so far as he was aware he had had no representation from the dairy industry council on-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe I had from the dairy council. I thought it was the federation of agriculture to which reference was being made. But I believe I did have representations from the dairy council.

I have had representations from the dairy industry in my own constituency and, although I cannot state it as a fact, it is my understanding that they had written to the minister suggesting either a customs tariff or an excise tax on imported oils. I have no desire to return to the discussion of the excise tax resolution, but I wonder if the minister would tell us the attitude of the government in the matter. I was greatly impressed by the argument put forth this afternoon by the hon. member for Danforth. What he said certainly covered the situation in the dairy industry, and the whole question of this very cheap substitute product coming into the market. I am more particularly concerned because of the argument which, on the face of it, is hard to meet, namely that margarine affords a cheap substitute for butter, and that therefore it is wrong to do anything which would increase the price.
It seems to me that argument is completely removed when we find that the margarine producers put up their price to the extent of about ten cents a pound simply because the price of butter went up, despite the fact that the cost of production of margarine had not increased.

I strongly urge the minister to look into this situation. If he finds that the margarine manufacturers are taking advantage of the consuming public in this way it should influence his decision as to whether or not the national treasury should derive some revenue from their imports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The whole question will be studied, as to whether further protection should be afforded the dairy industry by substantially increasing the barriers to the importation of margarine or its ingredients from other countries.
I believe I should say however that it was our general feeling we should not take action of that kind while the proceedings at Torquay were under way. I am one who believes that the results achieved at Geneva and at Annecy should have substantial influence and were responsible to a substantial degree for the marked improvement in our balance of trade with the United States. I indicated before that in my opinion we have obtained a very satisfactory trade agreement at Torquay. I hope the house will agree with that when they see the results.
So, speaking generally, I felt and my colleagues felt it would be extremely unfortunate to take any action by imposing any further barriers to a free flow of trade between countries when we were arguing strenuously at Torquay for a lowering of those barriers.
It is not an easy problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a difficult problem, as the hon. member knows.

But the particular thing that irritates me is the fact of their increasing their price without apparently any excuse or any increased cost, just because the price of butter went up as the result of an unexpected development in the supply of butter.

There are several questions I should like to put to the minister. The first has to do with the country or countries from which most of these commodities which are the subject of decreases in tariff come. Will the minister indicate what countries will benefit from the proposed reductions in tariff rates, or those which will principally benefit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I think I indicated in my remarks on the budget, the principal reductions are in the agricultural implement field, diesel engines for use in fishing vessels, mining equipment and certain plastic items. Those items in the agricultural implement field will come mostly from the United States.
Customs Tariff
The mining equipment would come principally from the United States with some from the United Kingdom. I think it is fair to say that most of that type of equipment *comes from the United States. The diesel engines would come from the United Kingdom and the United States, but I would think the United Kingdom would have a decided edge because of the preferential rate. The plastic items would come principally from the United States, but the United Kingdom would also be able to avail itself of the reduced rates.
It is quite clear that the United States will be the chief beneficiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Others will be as well, but the United States is the principal supplier of these things.
We are dealing with them in general terms. I was under the impression, which the minister has now confirmed, that the United States will be the chief beneficiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that they are not broad reductions.
The United States will be the chief beneficiary of the proposed reductions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Canadian consumer will be the chief beneficiary, if I may say so.

There are two sides to this. I was thinking in terms of benefits to the producers. Obviously these benefits will flow chiefly to the United States. For that reason it surprises me to hear the minister say that the United States were not interested in any bargaining at Torquay with respect to any of these items. Knowing how astute the United States businessman is and how ready his government is to further his interests it seems unusual to me that the United States were not prepared to do some bargaining in return for the benefits to the United States producers which these proposed reductions offer.
My second inquiry is as to the estimated loss of revenue to the Canadian treasury from the proposed reductions. The minister may wish to indicate at the same time what increase in revenue is contemplated from such increases in the tariff rates as are involved in the present proposals. Perhaps he could then give the net figure, the overall estimated reduction in revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid the only increase is, as I indicated before, in the plastic items. I am sorry that no estimates have been made as to the increases in revenue which would result. Similarly it is hard to estimate with any degree of accuracy what decrease in

Customs Tariff
revenue there will be. However, it will be quite small in our picture. Of course, it is important to the people who have to import these articles. The fisherman who has to import a diesel engine for his boat and the farmer who has to import a milking parlour or some of these other things finds that it is quite important, but in the aggregate customs revenue it is pretty insignificant. Perhaps I could have an estimate made and give it to my hon. friend when we are in committee on the bill.

My next question has to do with the application of the Geneva agreements, if at all, to the proposed reductions. What application will the Geneva agreements have to the reduced rates that are proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If any of these rates are below the rates fixed in the Geneva agreements, we are not to be bound. However, we are free to go back to the rates stipulated in the Geneva agreements. We are free under the Geneva agreements or the Annecy agreements, and again under the Torquay agreements, to make reductions in tariff rates without in any way impairing the validity of the agreements, but we are bound not to make increases without complying with whatever the formalities are under the agreements.
To how many commodities on which it is proposed to reduce the tariff rates do the Geneva agreements apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that some of them will probably be covered in part, but there are no complete items.

My next inquiry has to do with the timing of the present resolution. In his budget speech, as reported on page 1813 of Hansard of April 10, the minister made reference to the tariff negotiations which had been taking place at Torquay during the past six months and said:
It has been arranged between the countries represented at Torquay that the details of the agreements resulting from the negotiations will be announced by the participating governments on May 9. Consequently I am not in a position to review the results at this time.
It would only be a matter of speculation until we know more about the results at Torquay as to what effect the Torquay agreements may have on any of these items, or what the result may be to the general picture of trading between one country and another in respect of tariff concessions. I am not proposing to ask the minister to delay the adoption of this resolution, but in order that the matter may have adequate consideration I wonder if he will agree that he will not move second reading of his bill to amend the Customs Tariff until after May 9?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is an entirely appropriate suggestion and I shall be happy to do that. I think it will be most helpful if the house could study the bill after the details of the Torquay agreements have been announced. I think that would be an excellent way to proceed.
They will be announced next Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the ninth; yes, next Wednesday. I doubt if we would get to it before that.

There is one other matter I should like to mention to the minister, and with approval. The minister may wish to send for smelling salts or something else to overcome the effects of surprise. I should like to mention item 705 in which the minister proposes to extend the period within which settlers may bring in their effects and still have them treated as settlers' effects. It seems to me that this is a most praiseworthy move. I cannot think of anybody whom it is going to hurt, and I can think of it bringing considerable assistance to many people who otherwise would suffer grave inconvenience and perhaps loss by reason of the present provision which it is now proposed to change. I do not know how large this item bulks in the total fiscal picture or the total trade picture, but it seems to me it is one to which the house will be glad to give approval.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for his congratulations. I agree with him. I think it is a most desirable item. It was made at the suggestion of my colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I have an amendment to the wording of the proviso in item 705 which I shall ask one of my colleagues to move. It broadens its application to include those settlers who have come in during the last three years. We have had it under examination a little more closely than we had been able to at the time the budget resolutions were introduced. I am wrong. It includes those who came in as far back as the end of the last war. I thought it was only three years.
Better still.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That amendment will be moved when we reach that item. It is merely an amendment to the wording to broaden it to that extent.

Some two or three months
ago I brought to the minister's attention the question of the customs duty on ground bagged clays or bentonites which are used in the manufacture of drilling mud, a necessary substance in the drilling of oil and gas wells at the present time. The situation with

respect to this substance is that quite a flourishing small industry manufacturing this drilling mud has been built up in Calgary. Its product was much used throughout the province of Alberta. The shipping in of ground bagged clays or bentonites from the United States has now practically put that concern out of business. They have requested that some protection should be afforded. I have looked through these tariff items quite carefully, and I have not been able to find any mention of these bagged clays. I wonder if the minister would tell us what decision he came to and why no action was taken in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I gave consideration to my
hon. friend's representations, but for the same reason that precluded my giving active consideration to increases in the duties on vegetable oils or other items, because the tariff negotiations at Torquay were pending, it was decided that this year no increased duty could be put on.

That means essentially
then that consideration is really deferred for another year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I want to
ask the minister what will happen with respect to the Torquay agreement. What will be its legal status when it arrives here and is presented to this house? Will it need legislative implementation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that, as was
the case with the Geneva and Annecy agreements, it does not require immediate legislative implementation, but the intention would be that it would eventually receive that. Our attitude has been that we would not hurry our legislative implementation until we saw that formal legislative implementation was being carried through in other jurisdictions, and that is the present status of Geneva and Annecy. It can be put into effect by executive action.
None of these trade agreements have ever been approved formally by parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that is correct.

How long ago is it that the
Geneva agreement was negotiated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Four years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Are we in Canada waiting
for the United States?
Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are waiting to see what
they do. In the meantime we have got substantial benefits under the agreements.
Does the minister expect there will be legislation in the near future on any of these agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just when I cannot say. I doubt if there would be legislation at this session.

From the minister's answer to the hon. member for Greenwood, I am not quite clear as to what part of the Torquay agreement, if any part, may be brought into operation in Canada apart from parliamentary action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, tariff reductions can be brought into effect by order in council. That has always been our law. On the other hand, tariff increases have to come to the house.

Are we to assume then that parliament is not going to be afforded an opportunity of passing on the Torquay agreement, save perhaps incidentally in some discussion here, and that, as it may be assumed that it will involve only reductions on Canada's part and no increases in our tariff, the whole agreement so far as Canada is concerned can be brought into immediate effect and operation, or into effect and operation at a later time, simply by executive decision without any expression of approval or otherwise on the part of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What we are required to do to implement our part of the agreement is to bring into effect such tariff reductions as we may have agreed to in consideration of the tariff reductions received from others. We can make those tariff reductions-and it is done continually-by order in council, and I think the same procedure will be followed here as was followed in the case of Geneva and Annecy. There will of course be, as there was in the case of these other agreements, ample opportunity for discussing the terms and so on in the house.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give an undertaking as to when.
When was there an opportunity for discussing these other agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suppose I have not really given much thought to that. I know that Geneva and Annecy have both been discussed here in general terms. I suppose they could be discussed on the estimates of the Department of National Revenue. I think it would be proper to discuss their

Customs Tariff
general effect there. However, I would have to give some consideration to that. I am informed-I had forgotten-that the Geneva schedules were referred to committees of both the Senate and the House of Commons.
They were never formally approved in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possibly we might give consideration to referring the new schedules in the same way.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad this subject has arisen because, while it seems to be apparent from what the minister has said that no increases in the Canadian tariff will be called for by the Torquay agreements-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

-and only decreases will be required, the minister has indicated that legally these agreements may be brought into effect by executive decision without any formal approval on the part of parliament. I do not think that is a satisfactory state of affairs.
Those of us who sat in the last parliament will well recall that in November, 1947, a great to-do was made by the government about calling parliament in great haste to meet in Ottawa. The reason given at that time by the Prime Minister in a public statement for summoning parliament to meet about the first of December, 1947, a most unusual time, was not, as a matter of fact to give legislative effect to the radio budget introduced by the Minister of Finance, but was to lay before parliament for parliament's decision the agreements reached at Geneva.
We met at that time, and the Geneva agreements were not submitted to parliament for approval. As a matter of fact parliament has never yet been asked to give its sanction to the Geneva agreement. The minister has said that the schedules to the Geneva agreement were referred to a committee. They were referred to the banking and commerce committee but, if my memory serves me correctly as a member of that committee, those schedules were never reported out of the committee. They were allowed to die there in the spring of 1948. So far as debate is concerned, I recall one debate. It was one of those indirect debates. It may have been on a motion to refer to the committee, which did not afford an opportunity of bringing the important question of ratification to a neat issue before the house.
I say to you, sir, that the Geneva agreements have never been submitted to parliament in any fashion that would enable parliament to express its opinion upon them.

Similarly the Annecy agreement has never been submitted to parliament under any conditions which would enable parliament to express its approval or otherwise. It gives me a good deal of disappointment to hear an indication from the Minister of Finance tonight that parliament is not to be afforded an opportunity to deal specifically with the Torquay agreements, which we understand to be important, and express in the only way parliament can really express itself, its approval or disapproval of those agreements, by means of a direct vote on that particular issue.
In reviewing the whole situation, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me far too many of these tariff concessions arising out of international agreements have been carried out simply by executive decision. Parliament has been ignored with regard to them. If those agreements are as important as I think most, if not all, hon. members regard them, then surely the very least that should be required of the government is that those agreements should be submitted to parliament in such form and under such circumstances that a discussion can be held directly on the agreements and parliament may express either its approval or disapproval by a direct vote on that particular issue. If parliament does not have that opportunity then it seems to me parliament must review the whole basis on which tariff negotiations at these multilateral conferences are carried on, and recast the whole basis of their implementation by executive action. In matters so important as these it seems to me a crass neglect of the responsibility and supremacy of parliament that parliament should be by-passed and have no more opportunity to pronounce a direct verdict or judgment upon them than by some incidental, oblique kind of discussion on a motion to go into supply, or something of that nature. That does not offer a sufficiently direct opportunity to review these questions.
I think one might also say that in recent years there never has been enough time spent in parliament in the discussion of trade policies. Usually what little opportunity has been afforded to discuss trade matters has been on bills such as this involving minor, and sometimes quite trivial, amendments to the customs tariff. Trade policies are far too important to be so treated. Looking forward now to the time when these Torquay agreements are to be introduced, and assuming they will have the importance we have been led to attach to them, it seems to me that here is an occasion when the government should afford the house, at the earliest convenient time, an opportunity of discussing those agreements and the whole trade

picture in general, which is not free of disturbing factors. At page 1799 of Hansard, in his budget speech, the minister referred to an improved regional trade position in these words:
As a result of these shifts in trade our regional trade became much better balanced.
I think we are all glad to see the United States purchasing more from Canada. We should like to see a much closer balance between our exports to and imports from that country; but no one can survey the over-all trade picture in the world today without feeling very grave concern about the way our sales to the United Kingdom, to the colonial empire and to many of the countries of Europe have undergone a serious reduction in recent years.
I mention that, Mr. Chairman, by way of urging upon the minister and the government that the introduction in the house of the Torquay agreements at a convenient opportunity be made the occasion of a debate on trade, on a motion by the government calling upon the house to give a direct expression of approval or otherwise to those agreements, so the matter may be brought to an issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be very happy to bring my hon. friend's suggestion to the attention of my colleagues, to see whether, if the business of the house permits it, his suggestion can be adopted.

I would like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton. I recall that the Geneva trade agreements were referred to the banking and commerce committee in 1947. There was quite a long discussion; we ran right through them, but it was finally decided not to put a motion for approval, so the Geneva trade agreements were not approved by that committee. I think the reason was obvious. There was a great deal of criticism of various sections of those agreements.
I recall that there were a number of escape clauses in both the Geneva and Annecy agreements, and I think it is correct to say that many nations have already committed a breach of many of the principles embodied in those agreements. It may be argued, of course, that they are still acting under the escape clauses, but the deadline for those clauses I think in some cases is 1951 and in others 1952. I want to know what will happen after those deadlines, as far as the nations still operating under those escape clauses are concerned. Will those nations be allowed to continue to operate under them even after the deadlines have
Customs Tariff
expired, or will they be called upon to fulfil their obligations under those trade agreements?
I have particularly in mind the whole policy of non-discrimination. We have tried as far as possible to adhere to that general principle, though I think when we put restrictions upon imports from the United States we were really committing a breach of it. We have since removed that prohibition, but some countries in Europe are still continuing the policy of discrimination. What are we going to do in the future? Are we just going to let this situation drift, or are we going, by proclamation, to declare that we are no longer interested in that international trade organization as far as those general agreements are concerned?
I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Eglinton is very good, that there should be a general debate on this matter so we can be informed just what the situation is. At the present time we appear to be just drifting^ along, operating under trade agreements which have not been agreed to by this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am rather in agreement
with my hon. friend; I would be very happy to have such a discussion. I must say I think Canada has derived substantial benefits under these agreements. It is perfectly true, as the hon. member has indicated, that the policy of non-discrimination to which we attach such great importance, for reasons which are familiar to most hon. members, has not yet been possible for a good many countries including most of those in the sterling area. We still hope that result may be achieved. I must confess that I did not come fully prepared or briefed to discuss the Geneva agreements and the various escape clauses on this resolution tonight, but the suggestion that we should try to find some suitable occasion when we can discuss questions of trade policy in general is one to which I could certainly give most sympathetic consideration.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I see it is eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I guess we had better let it stand. If we could pass this resolution, of course we have the bill and we have to go through it item by item, but probably it is not appropriate to try to do that tonight.

I feel that
what the hon. member for Eglinton has said is fully warranted, and I welcome the minister's attitude. I do think we should

Customs Tariff
discuss this resolution a little longer, however. I believe the minister indicated that he would brief himself a little more fully, and the rest of us may do the same.
Could the minister, get information on any changes that have been made in the preference by executive action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I will have that information, either when we are back on the resolution or when we are on the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: So I may be clear on the matter of procedure, am I to understand that on this resolution a debate on the Geneva trade agreements is to be in order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. I am afraid I am not
prepared to discuss the Geneva agreement on this resolution. I do not believe my hon. friends were suggesting that, Mr. Chairman. I think both the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Acadia were urging that an appropriate opportunity should be afforded to discuss this matter generally, and in particular our obligations and rights under the Geneva agreement, but not on this resolution.
That is quite right, Mr. Chairman. What I was suggesting was that we need the Torquay agreement before us before we can undertake intelligently a discussion of that kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
What caused me
to make that remark was what the hon. member for Greenwood had said previously.
Shall I report progress and ask leave to sit again?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speechtext:

take up the estimates of the Department of Labour and of the Department of Resources and Development.
In that order?

It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
